headline_marked: [[Harry Kane wins Ballon d'Or]], first Englishman in 25 years, after scoring 73 goals
headline: Harry Kane wins Ballon d'Or, first Englishman in 25 years, after scoring 73 goals
summary: Harry Kane's remarkable season saw him score 73 goals in 65 games for Bayern Munich and England, culminating in football's highest individual honor. Alexia Putellas also secured her third women's Ballon d'Or.
details: Harry Kane has been crowned the Ballon d'Or winner, becoming the first Englishman in 25 years to receive football's most prestigious individual award. The 33-year-old Bayern Munich forward triumphed over Lamine Yamal and Kylian Mbappe at the ceremony held in his native London.

Kane's exceptional performance last season included a remarkable 73 goals in 65 games for club and country. His prolific scoring helped Bayern Munich secure a league and cup double, and he also netted six times for England at the World Cup.

Accepting the award, Kane thanked his Bayern Munich teammates, acknowledging their role in pushing him to achieve this success. He expressed pride in his goalscoring consistency, which he believes has been elevated since his move to Bayern in 2023.

In the women's category, Spain's Alexia Putellas claimed her third Ballon d'Or, extending her country's dominance. Her leadership in Barcelona's Champions League victory before joining London City Lionesses was key to her win.

Other notable awards included Luis de la Fuente named men's coach of the year for leading Spain to World Cup glory, and Barcelona's Pere Romeu for women's coach. Arsenal's Bukayo Saka received the Socrates award for his humanitarian work.

The ceremony, the first ever on English soil, experienced a nearly hour-long delay due to London traffic. Despite the initial hiccup, it concluded with a celebratory moment for the hometown hero, Kane.

headline_marked: [[59 foreign nationals executed in Saudi Arabia]] in 6 months amid concerns over unfair trials
headline: 59 foreign nationals executed in Saudi Arabia in 6 months amid concerns over unfair trials
summary: The alarming rise in executions, particularly for drug offenses, highlights issues of judicial transparency and limited defense opportunities for migrant workers.
details: Saudi Arabia has seen an alarming increase in executions of foreign nationals, with two Bangladeshis recently among them. In the first six months of this year alone, 59 foreign citizens faced capital punishment, raising global concerns.

The case of an Ethiopian prisoner executed last May illustrates the grim reality. He called his mother to say goodbye, and after his execution, his body was never returned to the family, leading to his mother's severe mental distress.

An Ethiopian community member shared this story with Amnesty International, stating, "They are not just killing our brothers; they are killing us too." Currently, 58 Ethiopians are on death row in Saudi Arabia's Khamis Mushait prison.

Foreigners are disproportionately affected by death penalties in Saudi Arabia. Amnesty International reports that nearly 75% of the 597 drug-related executions between January 2014 and June 2025 were foreign nationals.
Data from the Berlin-based ESOHR shows that 59 out of 108 executions in the first half of this year (January-June) were foreigners, accounting for about 54% of all capital punishments.

Among those executed for drug offenses in the last decade, 155 were Pakistani, 66 Syrian, 50 Jordanian, 39 Yemeni, 33 Egyptian, 32 Nigerian, 22 Somali, and 13 Ethiopian, according to Amnesty. The number of Pakistani citizens executed surpassed that of Saudi citizens.

Amnesty acknowledges its data relies on publicly disclosed executions, suggesting the true number may be higher. The organization demands an independent and transparent investigation into potential discrimination at every stage of the judicial process for foreigners.

The vulnerability of these migrant workers often begins before they even leave their home countries, through fraudulent recruitment practices. In Saudi Arabia, the Kafala (sponsorship) system further exacerbates their precarious situation.

The Kafala system is described as a restrictive and exploitative migration framework that disproportionately impacts migrant workers from African and Asian countries. Some accused individuals have reported being forced to carry illegal drugs, claims which courts reportedly did not investigate.

UN human rights experts have also noted the disproportionate impact of the death penalty on foreign nationals. This situation raises serious questions about fair trial standards and human rights for the large migrant population in Saudi Arabia.
